title: Worry Parking: a place to park your worries before bed
description: Write down the worry that keeps circling, park it, and face it for 15 minutes at your Worry Time. Built on worry postponement from CBT. All free.

problem.title: Lights off, worries on?
problem.text: The second your head hits the pillow, it starts: something you said today, tomorrow's meeting, the text that still hasn't come back. Telling yourself to stop thinking only makes it louder. Worry Parking doesn't ask you to push it away. You write it down, give it a spot, and set aside a time to deal with it.

features.title: Write it down, and it gets out of your head
features.text:
Write it exactly the way it sounds in your head, then rate how loud it is from 1 to 5. Tear off the ticket and the worry stays in the lot, blurred out.
If it drives back into your head, tell it: you already have a spot. There's a time for it, and it isn't now.

features.title: Face it for 15 minutes at Worry Time
features.text:
Every day at your Worry Time, you get a reminder. At the Exit Gate you read the worry again, check whether it actually happened, and see how loud it is now.
Then let it go, turn it into one small next step, or park it again until the next Worry Time.

features.title: See how often your worries came true
features.text:
As reviewed worries add up, the Exit Log shows what share actually happened and how much their level dropped.
Worry tends to predict the future as worse than it turns out. The more you log, the less you believe the next one.

items.title: Pick your Worry Time
items.text: The first time you open it, choose when you'll face your worries each day. You can change it later in Settings.

items.title: Park one real worry
items.text: Park something on your mind right away and notice how its level changes before and after.

items.title: Allow pickup reminders
items.text: At Worry Time you get a reminder with just the spot number.

reference.title: Why it works
rows: People who moved their worrying to a short daily worry period spent less time worrying and reported less anxiety and fewer sleep problems. (Borkovec et al., 1983; McGowan & Behar, 2013)
Write it down to put it down

Making a concrete plan stopped unfinished tasks from intruding on people's thoughts, and five minutes of writing before bed helped people fall asleep faster. (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011; Scullin et al., 2018)
When people with chronic worry tracked their worries, 91% of them didn't come true. (LaFreniere & Newman, 2020)
reference.note: Worry Parking is built on worry postponement, a technique from cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) that has been studied for decades.

items.q: How do I change my Worry Time?
items.a: Go to Worry Time in the Settings tab. The new time applies to worries you park from then on. Worries already parked keep their original exit time.

Check Notifications in the Settings tab. If it says notifications are off, tap Open iOS Settings and turn them on. With a Focus or Do Not Disturb on, reminders may arrive silently. Even without a reminder, worries that are due show as ready for pickup in the lot.

items.q: Can people see my worry in the notification?
items.a: No. Notifications only show the spot number, like "P3 is ready for pickup". The worry itself only appears once you open the app and enter the Exit Gate.

items.q: Can I look at a worry before Worry Time?
items.a: Tap its car in the lot and choose Send it to the exit gate now. Postponing works best when you wait, though. Most worries feel smaller by Worry Time.

items.q: Can I move my records to a new iPhone?
items.a: Everything is stored only on your iPhone, with no account or sync. Restoring a new iPhone from an iCloud or computer backup, or using Quick Start, brings it over along with your other app data.

items.q: How do I delete my records?
items.a: In the Exit Log tab, swipe left on an entry to delete it. Deleting the app removes everything.
Worry Parking is a self-help tool based on worry postponement from CBT. It is not a medical device and does not replace professional diagnosis or treatment.

If worry is getting in the way of daily life, or you're having thoughts of hurting yourself, please don't carry it alone. Reach out to a mental health professional, call or text 988 in the US, or contact your local emergency services.
